newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ambitious Asian nuclear agenda boils down to cash.
newsitem.headline: Ambitious Asian nuclear agenda boils down to cash.

text.p: Asia's nuclear power development has fallen well behind the pace set by bold government projections -- and safety concerns have less to do with it than a lack of cold, hard cash, analysts say.

The technology's high price tag, they say, is why some Asian countries are years behind -- with hundreds of billions of construction dollars to go -- in the ambitious schedules they've charted to power themselves into the 21st century.

"If you look at the facts on a plant-by-plant planning basis, it's clear that many government projections outpace reality," said Ron Hagen, Nuclear Energy Analyst at the Honolulu-based East-West Center.

While the capital cost for new nuclear facilities can run as much as four times higher than alternative coal or gas fire plants, Hagen says concerns over the security of global hydrocarbon reserves galvanize Asian policymakers to plan big now and pay big later.
"The problem has been and continues to be money," he said.
Atsushi Kido, Senior Economist at Japan's Institute of Energy Economics (IEE) echoed the views.
"Government projections, including Japan's, are more like ideal goals to be reached than realistic assessments," Kido said.
"Governments come up with targets based on the electricity demand projections, but funding to achieve the target has not always been taken care of," he added.
Estimates differ, but analysts say the capital costs of constructing 1 megawatt of capacity can roughly be seen at $2 million to $3 million, or $2 billion $3 billion per gigawatt (GW).
According to a recent IEE study, South Korea, Taiwan, China, India, and Pakistan plan to have a combined 53 gigawatts of nuclear generation capacity by around the year 2010.
But the group has just 19 GW of capacity at present and just 10.5 GW worth of capacity under construction.

That means the countries must locate sites and carry out construction of some 23 GW -- worth $50 billion to $70 billion -- in less than 13 years. Analysts say facilities can take seven to ten years to complete.
Japan vowed last week to press ahead with its plans to add some 27 new GW, or $50 billion to $80 billion, worth of new capacity by 2010, atop the 40 GW it possesses now.

The government reassurances, which came in spite of the intense public scrutiny Japan's nuclear program has drawn to itself via a series of accidents and failed cover-ups, also followed a decision by France a day earlier to abandon its $10.5 billion fast-breeder reactor (FBR) program.

Both countries had made multi-billion dollar wagers over the last 25 years that FBR technology, which theoretically produces more plutonium than it consumes, would play a leading role in supplying their future energy needs.

But France's June 20 decision, and attendant comments by the French environment minister which labeled the program a "stupid financial waste"-- leaves Japan as the only country in the world actively pursuing FBR technology.
